title: NAB calls in McKinsey and KPMG for corporate and insto bank review
full_text:
National Australia Bank is taking a page out of ANZ’s book, following the rival lender’s decision to call in McKinsey consultants for advice.
This time last year, ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos announced sweeping changes at the bank which saw 3500 jobs axed. Matos had McKinsey run the ruler over the business before revealing a major strategy refresh to shareholders in October that was largely well received.
NAB had both McKinsey and KPMG looking at its corporate and institutional division. Penny Stephens
Last week, it emerged NAB was in the midst of a major restructure of its corporate and institutional bank. And who was helping NAB, according to people briefed on the engagement who requested anonymity given they were not authorised to comment publicly? McKinsey.
McKinsey was tasked with comparing the NAB unit to its big four and global counterparts, these people said. The scope of McKinsey’s review for NAB was far smaller than its work at ANZ and lasted a few weeks.
NAB’s recent job cuts were not explicitly dictated by the McKinsey findings, but the review’s broader suggestions were considered by executives before they finalised the restructure.
The McKinsey engagement comes after NAB had another major consultancy, KPMG, review workflows and role responsibilities within a subsection of the department’s corporate finance division in May.
As previously revealed, around 68 bankers, including those with day-to-day contact with NAB’s biggest clients, had their roles changed or culled last week. Net departures came in at about eight after redeployment, but the sheer scale of the overhaul surprised many of the bank’s staff.
Although the impacted staff were not at the executive general manager level, many were “heads of” particular sectors. These are the equivalents of managing directors or rainmakers at large global investment banks.
Ahead of this year’s reporting season, Goldman Sachs warned of 35 ASX-listed companies where a wave of job cuts is likely, among them was NAB. The list focused on firms where labour costs are at least 10 per cent of sales, and have risen at least 10 per cent since 2022.
“NAB, like many large organisations, may engage external consultants from time to time to support or provide guidance on programs of work, particularly to better understand market benchmarks, best practice or to access specialist capability,” a spokesman said.
